note: Hand-written Grade 5 Core-word content, layered over the draft so it always wins. Cast is Grade 5's own, derived from its readings: Amal, Nora, Sami, Teacher Yasmin, Leo, Talia, Zara, Noah, Daniel, Maya, Jamal, Hana, Kobi. Sentences are capped at 100 characters and 17 words, which is Grade 5's own measured maximum — the grade teaches text forms, so its examples are prose rather than the short modelling sentences of the lower grades.

acceptance.childMeaning: Agreeing to something, or coming to terms with it.
acceptance.repitchedFrom: grade 8: 'The act of allowing or agreeing to something, often without questioning it' — the trailing clause makes acceptance sound like a failure to think, which is the opposite of what this unit teaches about coming to terms with a loss.
practiceSentences: Her acceptance of the apology ended the quarrel.
What helps a person reach acceptance after a loss?
The club sent a letter of acceptance to every applicant.
Acceptance does not mean you agree with everything.
The fable ends in acceptance rather than revenge.

accordingly.childMeaning: In a way that fits what has just been said.
practiceSentences: The forecast was poor; accordingly, we changed the route.
She read the rules and acted accordingly.
Accordingly, the meeting was moved to Thursday.
He knew the risk and prepared accordingly.
The fable ends badly, and the villagers behave accordingly after.

acid.childMeaning: A sour substance that can burn or dissolve other materials.
practiceSentences: Lemon juice is a weak acid.
Which acid is used in a car battery?
Strong acid must be handled with gloves.
Acid rain wears away stone over many years.
The class tested each liquid to find the acid.

adaptation.childMeaning: A feature that helps a living thing survive where it lives.
practiceSentences: Thick fur is an adaptation to a cold climate.
Which adaptation helps this plant hold water?
Every adaptation has a cost as well as a use.
The camel's foot is an adaptation to soft sand.
Adaptation happens over generations, not in one life.

adequate.childMeaning: Good enough for what is needed, but no more.
adequate.repitchedFrom: grade 7: 'Good enough for what is needed; sufficient.' - it explains the word with `sufficient`, which is itself a Grade 5 Core word in unit 7, so the definition borrows a word the learner is separately being taught.
practiceSentences: The light was adequate for reading, but only just.
Is one blanket adequate for a cold night?
Her answer was adequate rather than impressive.
We had adequate food for three days.
Adequate is a low bar, not a compliment.

altitude.childMeaning: The height of something above sea level.
practiceSentences: The plane levelled off at a high altitude.
What altitude does this satellite keep?
Air grows thin at altitude, so breathing is harder.
The village sits at an altitude of 900 metres.
They measured the altitude with an instrument.
The reading stopped altogether after the storm.
How many samples were there altogether?
Altogether, the trip took nine hours.
She was not altogether sure of the result.
The old telescope was altogether too small.

ambition.childMeaning: A strong wish to achieve something important.
practiceSentences: Her ambition was to write a book of her own sheeko.
What ambition does the youngest son hold?
Ambition without patience rarely finishes anything.
His ambition grew after he met the visiting engineer.
The tale warns against ambition that forgets other people.

ambitious.childMeaning: Having a strong wish to achieve something difficult.
practiceSentences: The plan was ambitious for a class of ten.
Is that an ambitious target or a realistic one?
She is ambitious about her writing, and works at it.
An ambitious project needs an honest timetable.
Daniel set himself an ambitious reading goal.

antagonist.childMeaning: The character who stands against the main character.
practiceSentences: The antagonist blocks whatever the hero wants.
Who is the antagonist in this legend?
A good antagonist believes they are right.
The antagonist need not be a person at all.
Storm and hunger are the antagonist of that tale.

anxiety.note: Not a change from the Core-words work — a pre-existing fault in Grade 5's own vocabulary, surfaced by the cast check. Sentence 4 named Theo, who belongs to Grades 2 and 3 and appears nowhere in Grade 5's readings. Replaced with Noah, who does. This word is `reused` and already has audio, so the edit costs exactly one clip to re-record; the narration index marks it stale by itself.
practiceSentences: A small knot of anxiety sat in Amal's stomach as the concert began.
Taking slow, deep breaths can help you calm your anxiety before a test.
Have you ever felt anxiety before speaking in front of the whole class?
"Talking to my mum about my anxiety always makes me feel better," said Noah.
Nora's anxiety melted away when she saw her friends waving at the school gate.

extraSentences: Astronomy asks questions that take centuries to answer.

atom.childMeaning: The smallest particle of an element that can exist.
practiceSentences: Everything around you is built from atoms.
How small is a single atom?
An atom has a nucleus with electrons around it.
Two atoms of hydrogen join one of oxygen to make water.
No microscope can show you a single atom directly.

automatic.childMeaning: Happening by itself, without a person doing it each time.
practiceSentences: The gate has an automatic lock.
Is the reply automatic or written by hand?
Breathing is automatic; you do not decide to do it.
An automatic system still needs checking.
Her reaction was so quick it looked automatic.

carbon.childMeaning: An element found in every living thing, and in coal and diamond.
carbon.repitchedFrom: grade 2: 'Carbon is part of the name of a gas that trees take in from the air.' - that describes carbon DIOXIDE by way of its name, which is not what carbon is. At Grade 5 the word sits with atom, molecule and compound, where it is an element.
practiceSentences: Every living thing on Earth contains carbon.
Where is carbon found besides living things?
Diamond and coal are both made of carbon.
A carbon atom can join with four others.
Burning fuel releases carbon into the air.

characterisation.childMeaning: The way a writer shows what a character is like.
practiceSentences: Her characterisation is done through small actions.
What characterisation do the first two pages give us?
Good characterisation shows rather than tells.
The characterisation of the trickster is the tale's best part.
Dialogue is a tool of characterisation.

climax.childMeaning: The most exciting or important point of a story.
practiceSentences: The climax comes when the two brothers finally meet.
Where is the climax of this tale?
Everything before the climax builds towards it.
A climax that arrives too early leaves nothing after.
The climax is short; the resolution follows it.

combustion.childMeaning: The process of burning, which gives out heat and light.
practiceSentences: Combustion needs fuel, heat and oxygen.
What happens to the fuel during combustion?
Combustion in the engine pushes the piston down.
Without oxygen, combustion stops at once.
The rocket rises on the force of combustion.

compound.childMeaning: A substance made when two or more elements join together.
compound.repitchedFrom: grade 6: 'Made by joining two or more smaller words or parts together.' - the WORD-FORMATION sense, which belongs in a spelling unit. Here the word sits with atom, molecule and acid, where a compound is chemical.
practiceSentences: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
Which compound forms when iron rusts?
A compound behaves differently from the elements in it.
Salt is a compound, not an element.
The class listed every compound they could name.

compromise.childMeaning: An agreement where each side gives up something.
practiceSentences: They reached a compromise before the bell rang.
What compromise would settle this fairly?
A good compromise leaves nobody entirely happy.
The brothers found a compromise over the land.
Compromise is not the same as giving in.

condensation.childMeaning: The change from a gas back into a liquid as it cools.
practiceSentences: Condensation forms on a cold glass on a warm day.
What causes the condensation on the window?
Clouds form by condensation high in the air.
Condensation is the opposite of evaporation.
Wipe the condensation away before you read the scale.

conscience.childMeaning: The sense inside you that tells you what is right and wrong.
practiceSentences: His conscience would not let him keep the money he had found.
What does your conscience tell you to do here?
Amal's conscience troubled her all week until she owned up.
A clear conscience is worth more than an easy escape.
The fable ends when the merchant finally listens to his conscience.

conscious.childMeaning: Aware of something, and able to think about it.
practiceSentences: She was conscious of every eye in the hall watching her.
Were you conscious of how quiet the room had become?
Sami made a conscious choice to speak more kindly.
The patient stayed conscious throughout the whole journey.
Being conscious of a habit is the first step to changing it.

considerable.childMeaning: Large enough to matter; a good deal of something.
practiceSentences: A considerable amount of rain fell overnight.
Was there considerable damage to the roof?
She showed considerable patience with the beginners.
The task took considerable time and care.
Considerable effort went into the display.

consideration.childMeaning: Careful thought, or care for other people's feelings.
practiceSentences: She showed consideration by keeping her voice low.
What consideration does a good neighbour show?
After long consideration, he changed his answer.
Consideration for others costs nothing at all.
The plan deserves proper consideration before a vote.

consistent.childMeaning: Always behaving or happening in the same way.
consistent.repitchedFrom: grade 8: 'Always behaving or happening in the same way, without contradicting itself.' - the trailing clause is a second, harder idea bolted onto a clear first one.
practiceSentences: Her handwriting is consistent from start to finish.
Are the readings consistent with yesterday's?
Consistent practice beats occasional bursts.
The rule must be consistent for everyone.
His story stayed consistent under questioning.

constructive.childMeaning: Helpful, and meant to improve rather than to knock down.
practiceSentences: Her comments were constructive and easy to use.
What makes criticism constructive?
A constructive suggestion offers a way forward.
Be constructive, even when you disagree.
The meeting was short but constructive.

contemporary.childMeaning: Belonging to the present time; modern.
contemporary.repitchedFrom: grade 7: 'Living or happening at the same time; modern.' - two distinct senses joined by a semicolon. The modern sense is the one this unit uses.
practiceSentences: The gallery shows contemporary painting.
Which contemporary writer do you enjoy?
Contemporary music sounds nothing like this.
A contemporary account is written at the time.
The building looks contemporary beside the old church.
The decision proved controversial across the whole town.
Why is this rule so controversial?
A controversial topic needs careful handling.
The referee made a controversial call.
Nothing controversial was said at the meeting.

convenience.childMeaning: The quality of being easy or useful to do or use.
practiceSentences: For convenience, the notes are stored in one folder.
Is the new timetable a convenience or a nuisance?
The convenience of a torch is that it fits a pocket.
She chose the later train for convenience.
Solar panels offer the convenience of free power.

conventional.childMeaning: Following the usual rules or traditions.
practiceSentences: She chose a conventional opening for her essay.
Is that the conventional way to do it?
Conventional methods are not always the best.
The design is conventional but very well made.
He gave the conventional answer and moved on.

conversely.childMeaning: Looked at the other way round.
practiceSentences: Cold air sinks; conversely, warm air rises.
Conversely, the smaller sample gave a clearer result.
She reads quickly; conversely, he takes his time.
Rain helps the crops; conversely, too much ruins them.
Conversely, a shorter route may take longer.

convincing.childMeaning: Good enough at explaining something to make you believe it.
practiceSentences: Her argument was clear and convincing.
Was the evidence convincing enough?
A convincing story keeps its details straight.
He gave a convincing account of what happened.
The excuse was not remotely convincing.

cooperation.note: Sentence 3 was 'Amazing cooperation, Sami!" shouted Nora as the windmill finally spun.' — a closing quotation mark with no opening one, so the sentence was broken on the page as written.
practiceSentences: Good cooperation helped the team finish before the deadline.
Why does cooperation matter so much during a group project?
"Amazing cooperation, Sami!" shouted Nora as the windmill finally spun.
Teacher Yasmin praised the cooperation between every table in the hall.
The tale teaches the value of cooperation, patience and steady work.

correspond.childMeaning: To match or agree with something else.
correspond.repitchedFrom: grade 7: 'To communicate by writing; to be similar to or match something.' - two unrelated senses joined by a semicolon, which asks one card to teach both. This unit puts the word beside data and measurement, so the matching sense is the one it needs.
practiceSentences: The bright dots correspond to the stars on the chart.
Which numbers correspond to the readings you took?
His results correspond closely with ours.
The colours correspond to different temperatures.
Make each label correspond to the sample it names.

courtesy.childMeaning: Polite behaviour that shows respect for others.
practiceSentences: He answered every question with unfailing courtesy.
What courtesy does a guest owe a host?
Courtesy costs little and is remembered long.
She thanked the driver as a matter of courtesy.
The sheeko praises courtesy shown to a stranger.

criticism.childMeaning: Saying what is wrong or weak about something.
practiceSentences: Her criticism was fair and easy to act on.
How do you take criticism without feeling hurt?
Useful criticism names the problem and the fix.
He offered criticism of the plan, not of the person.
Criticism stings less when you asked for it.

crucial.childMeaning: So important that everything depends on it.
practiceSentences: The next hour is crucial to the whole plan.
Why is this step crucial?
Water is crucial for every living thing.
Her evidence proved crucial at the hearing.
Timing is crucial when you bake bread.

definite.childMeaning: Certain and clearly decided, with no room for doubt.
practiceSentences: We need a definite answer before Friday.
Is that a definite plan or just an idea?
There was a definite improvement in her handwriting.
Nora gave a definite no, and would not be moved.
The story leaves no definite ending, which is the point.

density.childMeaning: How much mass a substance has for its size.
practiceSentences: Lead has a far greater density than wood.
What is the density of this sample?
A low density is why oil floats on water.
Density is mass divided by volume.
The density of the air falls as you climb.

desperate.childMeaning: So badly in need of something that you will try almost anything.
practiceSentences: The farmer grew desperate as the drought went on.
Why did the traveller make such a desperate choice?
In her desperate hurry she left the letter behind.
A desperate plan is rarely a wise one.
The fox in the tale becomes desperate and then dishonest.

determination.childMeaning: The quality of trying hard even when something is difficult.
determination.note: The inherited Grade 6 meaning was correct and ended without a full stop — the fourth such meaning found across these grades, after cooperate, announce and antonym.
practiceSentences: Her determination carried her through the long climb.
Where does that determination come from?
Talia showed real determination after failing twice.
Determination matters more than talent in this tale.
With quiet determination, Kobi finished what he had started.

dignity.childMeaning: A calm, serious manner that earns other people's respect.
practiceSentences: She accepted the result with great dignity.
How does the old woman keep her dignity in the story?
Losing well takes as much dignity as winning.
He spoke with the quiet dignity of someone sure of himself.
Every person deserves to be treated with dignity.

discipline.childMeaning: Training yourself to follow rules and keep working hard.
practiceSentences: Daily practice takes discipline more than talent.
What discipline does learning an instrument need?
The team's discipline showed in every match.
Sami built the discipline to write for ten minutes a day.
Discipline is choosing the harder thing when nobody is watching.

diverse.childMeaning: Made up of many different kinds.
practiceSentences: The class is diverse in every way that matters.
How diverse is the wildlife along this river?
A diverse group brings more ideas to a problem.
The island has a diverse range of plants.
Their diverse opinions made the debate lively.

diversity.childMeaning: The presence of many different kinds of people or things.
practiceSentences: The diversity of birds along the river surprised us.
How does diversity make a class stronger?
Our school celebrates the diversity of its families.
A forest's diversity protects it from disease.
Diversity of opinion makes a discussion worth having.

domestic.childMeaning: To do with the home, or with your own country.
practiceSentences: Domestic chores were shared between them all.
Is this a domestic or an imported product?
The cat is a domestic animal.
Domestic news filled the first three pages.
She wrote about domestic life in the 1950s.

dramatic.childMeaning: Sudden and striking, or to do with plays.
practiceSentences: There was a dramatic change in the weather.
Was the ending too dramatic to believe?
She made a dramatic entrance through the side door.
A dramatic pause can be worth a paragraph.
The dramatic society meets on Tuesdays.

ecology.childMeaning: The study of how living things relate to each other and their surroundings.
practiceSentences: Ecology looks at the whole system, not one animal.
Why does ecology matter to farmers?
Her interest in ecology began with a rock pool.
Ecology explains why removing one species matters.
The class studied the ecology of the riverbank.

educational.repitchedFrom: grade 8: 'Educational means designed to teach people something useful.' - it opens by restating the headword, which spends the first three words teaching nothing.
practiceSentences: The trip was enjoyable and genuinely educational.
What makes a game educational?
Educational television can be as good as a lesson.
The museum runs educational visits for schools.
She found the whole experience educational.

electrical.childMeaning: To do with electricity, or worked by it.
practiceSentences: An electrical fault stopped the whole experiment.
Which electrical parts does the circuit need?
Never touch electrical wires with wet hands.
The satellite runs on electrical power from its panels.
She drew the electrical circuit in her notebook.

embarrass.childMeaning: To make somebody feel awkward or ashamed.
practiceSentences: He did not mean to embarrass her in front of the class.
What would embarrass you most?
A gentle correction need not embarrass anyone.
She was careful not to embarrass the new pupil.
Do not embarrass a friend to get a laugh.

encouragement.childMeaning: Words or actions that give someone hope and confidence.
practiceSentences: A word of encouragement from Nora changed his whole day.
Who gave you the most encouragement this year?
She needed encouragement, not correction.
The crowd's encouragement carried the runners home.
Small encouragement at the right moment goes a long way.

equip.childMeaning: To supply somebody with the things they need.
practiceSentences: The school will equip the lab with new microscopes.
How do you equip a crew for six months in space?
They equip each boat with a radio and a flare.
Good notes equip you for the exam.
We must equip the team before the launch.

erosion.childMeaning: The wearing away of soil or rock by wind, water or ice.
practiceSentences: Erosion has cut a deep valley through the rock.
What causes erosion along this coast?
Tree roots slow erosion on a steep slope.
Erosion works over centuries, grain by grain.
The cliff path was closed because of erosion.

evolution.childMeaning: The slow change of living things over very long periods.
practiceSentences: Evolution explains why species differ from one another.
How does evolution happen so slowly?
Fossils give us evidence of evolution.
Evolution works over millions of years, not lifetimes.
The museum's display traces the evolution of the horse.

exceptional.childMeaning: Unusually good, or unusual in some way.
practiceSentences: Her memory for dates is exceptional.
Was this an exceptional case or a normal one?
Exceptional weather closed the road for a week.
He showed exceptional patience with the youngest.
An exceptional result deserves an explanation.

existence.childMeaning: The fact of being real, or of being alive.
practiceSentences: Nobody knew of the village's existence until the map was drawn.
Does the story prove the creature's existence?
The whole existence of the library depends on donations.
She led a quiet existence in a house beside the river.
Fossils are evidence of the existence of ancient life.
The external walls need painting.
Is the damage external or internal?
External advice can help you see a problem afresh.
The external temperature dropped sharply.
She wrote her notes on an external drive.

flashback.childMeaning: A scene that jumps back to something that happened earlier.
practiceSentences: A flashback shows us why he fears the water.
Where does the flashback begin?
The flashback explains the quarrel without stopping the story.
Writers use a flashback to fill in the past.
One flashback is enough for a short tale.

foreign.childMeaning: Belonging to a country that is not your own.
practiceSentences: She is learning a foreign language at evening class.
Which foreign country would you most like to visit?
The tale was translated from a foreign original.
Foreign coins filled the old tin.
A foreign word often keeps its own spelling.

forgiveness.childMeaning: Choosing to stop being angry with someone who wronged you.
practiceSentences: Forgiveness took him longer than an apology would have.
Is forgiveness always the right ending to a story?
She asked for forgiveness and meant it.
The fable turns on an act of forgiveness.
Forgiveness frees the person who gives it.

fossil.childMeaning: The preserved remains or trace of a living thing from long ago.
practiceSentences: The fossil was found deep in the cliff face.
How old is this fossil thought to be?
A fossil can be a bone, a shell or a footprint.
Each fossil is a record of a living thing.
Zara cleaned the fossil with a soft brush.

frequency.childMeaning: How often something happens in a given time.
practiceSentences: The frequency of the signal decides its pitch.
What is the frequency of these readings?
A higher frequency means more waves each second.
Storms rose in frequency over the decade.
Radios pick out one frequency from many.

frustration.childMeaning: Feeling upset or annoyed because you cannot do what you want.
frustration.note: Meaning kept. The Grade 6 sentences ran to 96 characters and were about soldiers banning gatherings and cancelling markets — that grade's own political material, and not this unit's subject.
practiceSentences: Amal felt a wave of frustration when the knot would not loosen.
How do you calm your frustration when a plan collapses?
"Let go of your frustration," the elder advised, "and think clearly."
Maya could not hide her frustration at the third failed attempt.
I felt real frustration after studying hard for the wrong chapter.

fundamental.childMeaning: Basic, and forming the foundation of something.
practiceSentences: Reading is fundamental to everything else at school.
What fundamental rule does the game rest on?
There is a fundamental difference between the two.
Fundamental skills need regular practice.
Trust is fundamental to any friendship.

galaxy.childMeaning: A huge group of stars, dust and gas held together in space.
practiceSentences: Our sun is one star in a galaxy of billions.
Which galaxy is nearest to our own?
A galaxy can take shapes like a spiral or a disc.
Light from a distant galaxy takes millions of years.
Sami drew the shape of our galaxy from memory.

generosity.note: Kept as it stands. `sheeko` is the unit's OWN term — its readings say "Somali storytellers call these tales sheeko" — and Jamal is Grade 5 cast, so neither is a stray from another grade.
practiceSentences: Sami thanked his neighbour for her generosity after the storm.
Why does generosity matter so much in this old sheeko, Amal?
What generosity you showed today, Jamal!
The tale ends by praising the young boy's generosity to strangers.
A sheeko might teach generosity, or courage, or respect for elders.

gradual.childMeaning: Happening slowly and steadily rather than suddenly.
practiceSentences: There was a gradual improvement over the term.
Was the change gradual or all at once?
A gradual slope is easier to climb than a steep one.
The gradual loss of light made reading hard.
Gradual progress is still progress.

grief.childMeaning: A deep sadness felt after losing someone or something dear.
practiceSentences: Her grief was quiet, and it lasted a long time.
How does the story show the shepherd's grief?
Grief comes in waves rather than all at once.
He carried his grief without letting it harden him.
Talking about grief makes it easier to bear.
"I have told you a million times" is hyperbole.
Which line is hyperbole rather than fact?
Hyperbole is not lying; nobody is meant to believe it.
The tale uses hyperbole to make the giant enormous.
A little hyperbole is funny; a lot is tiring.

ideal.childMeaning: The best or most perfect for a purpose.
ideal.note: Two faults, both in Grade 5's own reused content. The meaning ended without a full stop - the fifth such across these grades, after cooperate, announce, antonym and determination. And sentence 5 named Theo, who belongs to Grades 2 and 3 and appears nowhere in Grade 5's readings, exactly as `anxiety` did in unit 1. Replaced with Talia.
practiceSentences: Soft morning light is ideal for photographing birds.
What would your ideal Saturday morning look like?
A clear, moonless night is ideal for spotting stars.
"This shady spot is ideal for our picnic," decided Mum.
Talia found the ideal box for her rock collection.

immediate.childMeaning: Happening at once, with no delay.
practiceSentences: The medicine had an immediate effect.
Is an immediate answer really needed?
Her immediate reaction was to laugh.
The immediate danger had passed by morning.
We need an immediate decision about the trip.

impressive.childMeaning: So good that it makes people admire it.
practiceSentences: The finished model was genuinely impressive.
What is the most impressive thing you have built?
An impressive result came from very ordinary tools.
Her impressive memory saved the whole team.
The waterfall is impressive after heavy rain.

inadequate.childMeaning: Not good enough for what is needed.
practiceSentences: One blanket proved inadequate for that cold.
Was the lighting inadequate for reading?
Inadequate notes made the revision harder.
The old bridge is inadequate for heavy lorries.
An inadequate answer is worse than none at all.

initially.childMeaning: At the beginning, before things changed.
practiceSentences: Initially, nobody believed the shepherd's story.
What did you think initially?
She initially refused, then changed her mind.
The plan initially had three parts, not five.
Initially the tale seems simple, and it is not.

initiative.childMeaning: The ability to start something on your own without being told.
initiative.note: Meaning kept. The Grade 6 sentences ran to 110 characters, past this grade's cap of 100, and carried that grade's own material about a mayor, a flood and stranded families.
practiceSentences: Amal showed initiative by starting a blanket collection.
Why does initiative matter more than waiting to be told?
Taking the initiative, the volunteers mapped every safe route.
He took the initiative and planted trees along the path.
Initiative is doing the useful thing nobody asked for.

insecurity.childMeaning: A feeling of being unsure about yourself or your worth.
practiceSentences: His insecurity showed in the way he avoided the question.
What insecurity does the boastful lion hide?
Insecurity often sounds like showing off.
She admitted her insecurity about reading aloud.
Kindness costs little and eases another's insecurity.

intention.childMeaning: A plan or purpose you have in mind before you act.
practiceSentences: Her intention was kind, even though the result was not.
What was the traveller's intention in the fable?
Judge the intention as well as the outcome.
He had every intention of returning the book.
A good intention badly carried out still causes harm.
The internal walls are thinner than the outer ones.
Is the fault internal or external?
An internal check found the error first.
The clock's internal parts are very fine.
She kept her internal doubts to herself.

irony.childMeaning: When what happens is the opposite of what was expected.
practiceSentences: The irony is that the map led them home.
Where is the irony in this ending?
Irony can be gentle or bitter.
There is irony in a fire station burning down.
The reader sees the irony before the character does.

laboratory.childMeaning: A room fitted out for scientific work.
practiceSentences: The samples are kept in the laboratory fridge.
What rules apply in the laboratory?
A laboratory needs good light and running water.
She works in a laboratory studying soil.
Wear goggles whenever you enter the laboratory.

extraSentences: A legal ruling settled the argument over the land.

practiceSentences: Mars has ice caps; likewise, so does Earth.
She checked her figures, and Noah did likewise.
Likewise, the second sample gave no reaction.
The first test failed, and the second likewise.
Sound travels through water, and likewise through rock.

marvellous.childMeaning: Extremely good, in a way that causes wonder.
practiceSentences: The view from the hill was marvellous.
What a marvellous piece of work this is!
She has a marvellous memory for names.
The garden looked marvellous after the rain.
Kobi told a marvellous story about the old well.

maturity.childMeaning: Behaving in a sensible, grown-up way.
practiceSentences: She handled the disappointment with real maturity.
What maturity does the youngest brother show?
Maturity is not the same as age.
Admitting a mistake takes maturity.
Leo answered with a maturity that surprised everyone.

mental.childMeaning: To do with the mind or with thinking.
practiceSentences: She made a mental note of the address.
What mental skills does chess need?
Mental arithmetic is faster with practice.
The climb was a mental test as much as a physical one.
Mental health matters as much as physical health.

mindfulness.childMeaning: Paying calm, careful attention to the present moment.
practiceSentences: A minute of mindfulness settled the whole class.
How does mindfulness help before a test?
She practises mindfulness by noticing five sounds.
Mindfulness is noticing without judging.
The elder's mindfulness is what the sheeko admires.

mischievous.childMeaning: Fond of playful trouble, without meaning real harm.
practiceSentences: A mischievous grin spread across his face.
Was the puppy being mischievous or simply bored?
The mischievous twins hid every spoon in the house.
She gave a mischievous answer and then laughed.
Mischievous is not the same as unkind.

misunderstanding.childMeaning: A failure to understand something correctly.
practiceSentences: The whole quarrel began with one misunderstanding.
How could that misunderstanding have been avoided?
A single question would have cleared the misunderstanding.
Their misunderstanding lasted a week and cost a friendship.
Most of the fable's trouble comes from a misunderstanding.

molecule.childMeaning: A group of atoms joined together as one unit.
practiceSentences: A water molecule has three atoms.
How many atoms are in this molecule?
Molecules move faster when they are heated.
A single molecule is far too small to see.
Leo built a model of a molecule from clay and sticks.

mood.childMeaning: The feeling a piece of writing creates in the reader.
practiceSentences: The mood of the opening is calm and slow.
What mood do the short sentences create?
Weather is often used to set a mood.
The mood shifts the moment the drum stops.
Word choice changes mood more than plot does.

mutual.childMeaning: Felt or done by two people towards each other.
practiceSentences: Their respect was mutual from the start.
Is the agreement mutual, or one-sided?
They found a mutual friend at the market.
Mutual trust took years to build.
The decision was mutual, so neither resented it.

myth.note: Sentence 5 was 'If it does, the tale is probably a myth.' - the `it` refers to something in the passage it was mined from, and a card shows one sentence at a time.
practiceSentences: Every culture has at least one myth about how the world began.
Is this old tale a myth or a true historical event?
What a strange myth that turned out to be!
Amal wrote a myth explaining why the moon changes shape.
A myth explains the world through gods rather than evidence.

nonetheless.childMeaning: In spite of that; even so.
practiceSentences: The path was steep; nonetheless, they went on.
It rained all day; nonetheless, the fair opened.
Nonetheless, her argument deserves an answer.
He was tired, but nonetheless he finished.
The plan is risky; nonetheless, it may work.
An occasional visitor still knows the way.
Is that an occasional problem or a constant one?
Occasional rain broke the long dry spell.
She makes the occasional mistake, like anyone.
The occasional silence in a story is deliberate.

occupy.childMeaning: To fill a space, or to live or work in a place.
practiceSentences: Gas clouds occupy the space between the stars.
How much room does the telescope occupy?
Two families occupy the house beside the school.
The experiment will occupy the whole afternoon.
Dust and rock occupy the gaps in the ring.

occur.childMeaning: To happen, especially without being planned.
practiceSentences: Eclipses occur only when the moon lines up exactly.
How often does this occur?
Storms occur most often in the wet season.
A change like that does not occur overnight.
Errors occur when readings are taken in a hurry.

optimism.childMeaning: A habit of expecting good things to happen.
practiceSentences: Her optimism kept the group going through the rain.
Is optimism useful when a plan is failing?
Optimism is not the same as ignoring a problem.
Noah faced the long walk with steady optimism.
The ending rewards the farmer's patient optimism.

orbit.childMeaning: The curved path one object takes around another in space.
practiceSentences: The moon completes its orbit in about a month.
How long is the orbit of this satellite?
The rockets that carry them into orbit are marvels of engineering.
Earth's orbit around the sun takes a year.
A lower orbit means a faster journey round.
The overall effect is calm rather than tense.
What is your overall impression of the tale?
Overall, the plan worked better than expected.
The overall cost was lower than we feared.
Judge the overall shape before the details.

particular.childMeaning: One specific thing rather than any one.
practiceSentences: That particular line is the one to study.
Which particular version of the myth is this?
She has a particular way of ending a story.
Nothing in particular happened that afternoon.
He is particular about how the tools are stored.

peer.childMeaning: Someone of the same age or position as you.
practiceSentences: A peer can explain a puzzle better than an adult sometimes.
Who is your reading peer this term?
Peer pressure is hardest to resist when you are tired.
She read her draft aloud to a peer before handing it in.
Learning from a peer works both ways.

permanent.childMeaning: Lasting for ever, or for a very long time.
practiceSentences: The mark on the stone is permanent.
Is this a permanent change or a trial?
A permanent record outlives the person who made it.
She took a permanent post at the school.
Nothing in the tale turns out to be permanent.

perseverance.childMeaning: Keeping going even when something is difficult or slow.
practiceSentences: The tortoise wins the race through sheer perseverance.
What perseverance does learning a language need?
Her perseverance turned a weak draft into a strong one.
Perseverance is quiet, and it rarely gets applause.
Zara's perseverance finally opened the stiff old lock.

plot.childMeaning: The series of events that make up a story.
practiceSentences: A short, simple plot built around one clear problem.
How does the plot change after the storm?
In adventure writing the plot is full of action.
Summarise the plot in three sentences.
A plot needs cause and effect, not only order.

poetry.childMeaning: Writing arranged in rhythm or rhyme to express feeling powerfully.
poetry.note: The only mined sentence was 'Ehel Academy poetry collection Read the poem twice: once silently, once aloud.' - a page heading run together with an instruction, not a sentence at all.
practiceSentences: Poetry says a great deal in very few words.
What poetry have you learned by heart?
Reading poetry aloud changes how it lands.
Poetry does not have to rhyme.
The oldest poetry was spoken long before it was written.

predator.childMeaning: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
practiceSentences: The owl is a predator that hunts at night.
Which predator hunts here after dark?
A predator keeps the numbers of its prey in check.
Removing a predator can upset a whole habitat.
The cheetah is the fastest predator on land.

predictable.childMeaning: Easy to guess before it happens.
practiceSentences: The ending was predictable from the second page.
Is a predictable plot always a weak one?
His reaction was entirely predictable.
Predictable weather makes planting easier.
A myth is predictable because you have heard it before.

prejudice.childMeaning: An unfair opinion formed before you know the facts.
practiceSentences: Prejudice judges a person before meeting them.
How does the story challenge the villagers' prejudice?
She set her prejudice aside and listened properly.
Prejudice grows in the absence of real acquaintance.
The fable's lesson is that prejudice makes fools of us.

prey.childMeaning: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another.
practiceSentences: The hawk circled above its prey.
What prey does this snake hunt?
Prey animals often have eyes on the sides of the head.
When prey grows scarce, the hunter moves on.
Camouflage helps prey escape being seen.

principal.repitchedFrom: grade 6: 'The person in charge of a school, sometimes called a head teacher.' - the JOB TITLE. The supplied list places this word among the describing and evaluating words, so the adjective is the sense the unit needs; and `principal` meaning head teacher is not even the usual word in this course, which says head teacher throughout.
practiceSentences: The principal reason for the journey was hunger.
What is the principal difference between the two tales?
Water was the principal problem in the valley.
She played the principal part in the play.
The principal character is not always the narrator.

privilege.childMeaning: A special right or advantage only some people have.
practiceSentences: Sitting in the front row was a privilege, not a right.
What privilege does a library card give you?
She never treated her privilege as something earned.
It was a privilege to hear the elder speak.
Privilege is easiest to see when you do not have it.

protagonist.childMeaning: The main character, whose story the reader follows.
practiceSentences: The protagonist changes more than anyone else in the tale.
Who is the protagonist of this myth?
A protagonist need not be likeable.
The protagonist wants something and cannot easily get it.
Name the protagonist and the problem in one sentence.

radiation.note: Meaning kept. One Grade 6 sentence was about clean-up crews and containment near a grove - that grade's own material, and nothing to do with this unit.
practiceSentences: The sun gives off radiation that warms the Earth and lets plants grow.
How do astronauts shield themselves from radiation in space?
Too much radiation from the sun can burn your skin, the doctor said.
The ozone layer blocks a lot of harmful radiation.
Instruments on the probe measure the radiation around Jupiter.

extraSentences: A realistic story keeps to what could actually happen.

reflection.childMeaning: Light or sound bouncing back off a surface.
reflection.repitchedFrom: grade 5 UNIT 3: 'A short piece of writing where someone shares their thoughts and feelings about something that happened.' - the WRITING sense, correct in its own unit and wrong beside radiation, spectrum and solar. It came from this grade, one unit away, exactly as `pressure` and `life` did at Grade 4. Its fifth sentence was also the whole of 'This is a reflection.', which shows the word and teaches nothing.
practiceSentences: She saw her reflection in the still water.
What causes the reflection you see in a window?
A mirror works by reflection of light.
The reflection of the moon lay across the lake.
Sound bounces back too, and we call that reflection.

reliable.note: Sentence 4 named THEO, who belongs to Grades 2 and 3 and appears nowhere in Grade 5's readings. That is the THIRD stray Theo found in this grade's own reused content, after `anxiety` in unit 1 and `ideal` in unit 3. Replaced with Kobi, who is Grade 5 cast.
practiceSentences: My friend is reliable because she always helps me with my homework.
A reliable clock matters when the whole family rises early.
Which website gives the most reliable facts for our project?
"Kobi is reliable, so he will remember to feed the class fish," said the teacher.
The old bus is slow but reliable, arriving at eight every morning.

resilience.childMeaning: The ability to recover after something difficult.
practiceSentences: Her resilience after the setback impressed the whole team.
Where does resilience come from?
Resilience is built by small recoveries, not one big one.
The little tree's resilience is the point of the tale.
Daniel showed resilience by trying again the next morning.

resolution.childMeaning: The part of a story where the problem is settled.
resolution.repitchedFrom: grade 7: 'A firm decision or promise to do something.' - the NEW YEAR'S RESOLUTION sense. This unit sets the word beside climax, plot and protagonist, where the resolution is the ending that settles what the story raised. Both senses are real; the unit decides which one the card teaches.
practiceSentences: The resolution ties up every thread the story opened.
What resolution does the myth offer?
A rushed resolution leaves the reader unsatisfied.
In the resolution the brothers share the land.
Climax first, then resolution.

satellite.childMeaning: A machine sent into space to circle a planet and send back information.
practiceSentences: The satellite sends weather pictures back every hour.
Which satellite gave us this photograph?
A satellite must travel fast enough to stay in orbit.
The moon is a natural satellite of the Earth.
Nora tracked the satellite across the evening sky.

satisfaction.childMeaning: The pleasure of having done or got what you wanted.
practiceSentences: There is real satisfaction in finishing a long book.
What gives you the most satisfaction?
She looked at the mended fence with satisfaction.
Satisfaction comes from the effort, not only the result.
The work brought him quiet satisfaction.

scientific.childMeaning: Based on careful study, testing and evidence.
practiceSentences: A scientific answer can be checked by someone else.
What scientific evidence supports that claim?
The scientific method starts with a question.
Her approach was patient and scientific.
A myth is not scientific, and does not try to be.

self-esteem.childMeaning: The regard you have for your own worth.
self-esteem.note: Grade 5's only hyphenated Core word, the same shape as Grade 4's `self-control` and Grade 3's Africa/Asia/Europe. The build's masterFor lookup, the id and filename slug, and the word-check's inflection test all handle the hyphen now.
practiceSentences: Praise for effort builds self-esteem more than praise for talent.
How does failing affect your self-esteem?
Her self-esteem grew as her reading improved.
Low self-esteem can make a kind person seem unfriendly.
Self-esteem is not the same as boasting.

sensitivity.childMeaning: Being quick to notice and care about others' feelings.
practiceSentences: She spoke with real sensitivity about his loss.
What sensitivity does the storyteller show here?
Sensitivity to a friend's mood is a kind of listening.
His sensitivity made him a thoughtful reader.
Sensitivity can be a strength, not a weakness.
A severe storm closed the mountain road.
Was the punishment too severe?
Severe cold split the water pipes.
She gave him a severe look and said nothing.
The severe drought lasted three years.

shame.childMeaning: A painful feeling that comes from doing something wrong.
practiceSentences: Shame kept him silent when he should have spoken.
How does the character move past his shame?
There is no shame in asking for help.
Her face burned with shame at the memory.
Shame that leads to change is not wasted.

shoulder.childMeaning: The part where your arm joins your body, below your neck.
shoulder.note: The inherited sentences came from GRADE 1 and read as Grade 1: 'Put your hand on your shoulder.' / 'Can you tap your shoulder?' / 'Yes, I tap my shoulder!' Those are instructions for a five-year-old following a movement game, on a Grade 5 word card. The draft tool prefers a lower grade over a higher one because a simpler reading level is the safer failure - this is what that preference costs when it reaches four grades down.
practiceSentences: He carried the heavy sack on one shoulder.
Which shoulder did she injure in the fall?
The old man's shoulder ached before rain.
She looked back over her shoulder at the gate.
A hand on the shoulder can say more than words.

spectrum.childMeaning: The band of colours light splits into, or a full range of something.
practiceSentences: A prism splits white light into a spectrum.
Which colour sits at the end of the spectrum?
Astronomers read a star's spectrum to learn what it is made of.
A rainbow is a spectrum you can see from the ground.
The spectrum runs from red through to violet.

steam.childMeaning: The hot gas water turns into when it boils.
practiceSentences: If you lift the lid too early, the steam escapes.
What makes the steam rise from the kettle?
Steam turned the wheels of the earliest engines.
Steam is invisible until it cools into tiny droplets.
The steam clouded the cold window.

stereotype.childMeaning: A fixed, over-simple idea about a whole group of people.
practiceSentences: The story sets out to break a stereotype.
Which stereotype does this character disprove?
A stereotype ignores everything that makes a person themselves.
She refused to fit the stereotype anyone expected.
One example is never enough to justify a stereotype.

stomach.childMeaning: The part of your body where food goes after you eat it.
practiceSentences: Amal held her stomach, which had ached all night.
Why does your stomach growl when you are hungry?
"Eat slowly so your stomach can rest," said the doctor.
Fear can settle in the stomach before the mind names it.
The hero's stomach turned as the cave mouth darkened.
The rains came, and subsequently the river rose.
What happened subsequently to the youngest son?
She left early and subsequently missed the news.
The law was passed and subsequently ignored.
Subsequently, the two villages made peace.

suspense.note: Sentence 5 was 'Mystery stories are built on suspense.' - almost word for word the same as sentence 1, so the set of five taught four things.
practiceSentences: Mystery stories are built on suspense from the very first page.
How does the author create suspense in this chapter?
The suspense is unbearable, Maya, tell me what happens next!
A good film keeps the suspense going until the final scene.
Suspense comes from what the reader is not yet told.

symbolism.childMeaning: Using an object or image to stand for a bigger idea.
practiceSentences: The symbolism of the broken pot is clear by the end.
What symbolism does the river carry here?
Symbolism lets a story say two things at once.
A dove is the oldest symbolism for peace.
Not every object is symbolism; sometimes a pot is a pot.

temporary.childMeaning: Lasting only for a short time.
practiceSentences: The repair is temporary until the part arrives.
Is this a temporary or a permanent arrangement?
A temporary shelter went up beside the road.
Her sadness was real but temporary.
Temporary fixes have a way of lasting.

trustworthiness.childMeaning: The quality of being someone others can rely on.
practiceSentences: Her trustworthiness made her the obvious choice.
How is trustworthiness earned?
Trustworthiness shows in small promises kept.
The tale rewards trustworthiness above cleverness.
Nobody doubted Zara's trustworthiness.

ultimately.childMeaning: In the end, after everything else.
practiceSentences: Ultimately, the decision belongs to the whole class.
What ultimately changed the merchant's mind?
The plan was slow, but ultimately it worked.
Ultimately, a fable is an argument with a story around it.
She tried three routes and ultimately took the first.

universe.childMeaning: Everything that exists: all space, matter and time.
practiceSentences: The universe is far larger than anyone can picture.
How old is the universe thought to be?
Our galaxy is a very small part of the universe.
The universe is still expanding today.
Talia asked whether the universe has an edge.

vehicle.childMeaning: A machine such as a car or lorry that carries people or goods.
practiceSentences: No vehicle may pass the gate after dark.
What vehicle would you take across sand?
The vehicle was loaded before dawn.
A cart is the oldest vehicle of all.
Each vehicle must be checked before the journey.
The rocket must reach a huge velocity to escape Earth.
What velocity does the probe need?
Velocity is speed with a direction attached.
They measured the velocity of the falling weight.
A small change in velocity alters the whole orbit.

verse.childMeaning: A group of lines in a poem or song.
verse.repitchedFrom: grade 1: 'Verse means one part of a song or poem.' - correct and written for a five-year-old, and it opens by restating the headword.
practiceSentences: The second verse repeats the opening line.
How many verses does the song have?
Each verse ends with the same refrain.
She learned the first verse by heart.
A verse in a poem is like a paragraph in prose.

weathering.childMeaning: The breaking down of rock where it lies, by weather.
practiceSentences: Weathering cracks the rock before erosion carries it off.
How does frost cause weathering?
Weathering happens in place; erosion moves the pieces.
The statue's face was blurred by weathering.
Chemical weathering slowly dissolves limestone.

wellbeing.childMeaning: The state of being healthy, comfortable and happy.
practiceSentences: Sleep matters more to wellbeing than most people think.
What helps your wellbeing on a hard week?
The school looks after the wellbeing of every pupil.
Wellbeing is not only about the body.
Time outdoors improves the wellbeing of the whole class.

yacht.childMeaning: A light sailing boat used for racing or pleasure.
practiceSentences: The yacht leaned hard as the wind rose.
How many people can that yacht carry?
A yacht needs a deep keel to stay upright.
They watched the yacht round the headland.
The word yacht is spelled nothing like it sounds.
